query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of 5 vol% CoCrFeMnNi HEA nanoparticles to ZrB2, followed by spark plasma sintering at 1800 °C, will improve the strength, toughness, and structural integrity of ZrB2, reduce the required preparation temperature, and minimize the formation of holes and component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath.
generation.intervention: Addition of 5 vol% CoCrFeMnNi HEA nanoparticles to ZrB2, followed by spark plasma sintering at 1800 °C
generation.conditions: Under vacuum, with a heating rate of 100 °C/min and a pressure of 50 MPa
generation.structural_mediator: Uniform distribution of HEA nanoparticles at grain boundaries and within grains
generation.mechanism: Enhanced mechanical properties due to the uniform distribution of HEA nanoparticles, improved sintering kinetics, and reduced porosity
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength, toughness, and structural integrity, reduced holes and component failure, and lower required preparation temperature compared to conventional single-phase ZrB2
generation.baseline: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 ceramic prepared at temperatures above 2300 °C
generation.boundary: Preparation temperature, exposure time to liquid plating bath, and material composition
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount and distribution of the HEA additive, and the potential for the HEA additive to introduce new defects or impurities

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled preparation and testing of ZrB2-based composites with varying amounts and distributions of HEA additives
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain size, porosity, phase distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of HEA nanoparticles does not improve the mechanical properties and sintering kinetics of ZrB2, or if it introduces new defects or impurities that compromise the material's performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Medium-entropy alloys (MEAs), which consist of three to four elements, are derived from the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and demonstrate a mixing entropy ranging from 1 R to 1.5 R (where R represents the gas constant). Similar to HEAs, MEAs demonstrate superior mechanical properties, exceptional high-temperature stability, and improved corrosion resistance compared to conventional alloys []. Great attention has been paid to MEAs because of their excellent mechanical properties [,]. Laplanche et al. studied the equiatomic CoCrNi MEA produced by vacuum induction melting, which exhibited a single face-centered cubic (FCC) structure. This MEA exhibited an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 870 MPa, a yield strength (YS) of 360 MPa, and an elongation (El) of 38% at 293 K []. Moravcik et al. studied the equiatomic CoCrNi MEA through mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS). It exhibited a dual-phase, FCC (94.4%), and body-centered cubic (BCC) (5.6%) structure. The resulted UTS was 1024 MPa, and the El was 26% []. Non-equiatomic CoFeNi MEAs were prepared by Paganotti et al. using arc melting. These arc-melted MEAs exhibited high UTS and good plasticity []

Appropriate amounts of five powders were utilized to fabricate specimens of each composition (with the stoichiometry being calculated on the metal basis). The seven compositions are listed in Table 1 and referred to as HEB #1 to #7 in the text. The raw powders were mechanically alloyed via high energy ball milling (HEBM) using a Spex 8000D mill (SpexCertPrep, NJ, USA) for six hours in WC media. To prevent overheating, the HEBM was stopped every 60 minutes to allow cooling for five minutes. The powders were then hand ground in an agate mortar to a 325 mesh; subsequently, they were compacted into disks of 20-mm diameter and densified utilizing spark plasma sintering (SPS, Thermal Technologies, CA, USA) in vacuum (10−2 Torr) at 2000 °C for 5 minutes under a pressure of 30 MPa, with a heating ramp rate of 100 °C/min. In the present study, the effect of annealing on the microstructural and mechanical properties of HPT processed CoCrNi HEA was investigated. The results clearly indicate that the initial microstructure plays an important role in the mechanical properties of CoCrNi alloy. The initial microstructure with fine grain size of ~660 nm, high fraction of low angle grain boundaries, and high KAM value shows strain softening followed by strain hardening, whereas only strain hardening is observed for the microstructure with grain size >900 nm, a low fraction of low-angle grain boundaries, and low KAM value. The sample annealed at 700 °C for 15 min shows the optimized room temperature mechanical properties with a remarkable combination of strength (1090 MPa) and strain to failure (41%). Thus, the present study demonstrates that the severe plastic deformation followed by annealing is one of the effective ways of enhancing the mechanical properties in CoCrNi MEA.

These experimental results suggest that thermodynamic databases and models need to be extended and improved to better understand this complex kind of alloy. The observed phase instability of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA suggests that care needs to be given to the alloy in the exercise of temperature.
